title: What Women Most Desire
text:
In the days of King Arthur, a young knight of the court came upon a girl walking alone and raped her. The outcry was so great that he was sentenced to death. But the queen and her ladies begged the king to let them decide his fate. The queen told the knight she would spare his life if, within a year and a day, he could tell her what women desire most.

He wandered from place to place asking. Some said wealth, some honor, some fine clothes, some flattery, some to be free. No two agreed. As the year ran out, he came upon an ugly old woman sitting on a green at the edge of a forest. She promised him the true answer if he would grant the next thing she asked.

At court, he gave her answer: what women most desire is sovereignty, to have mastery over their husbands and over their own lives. No lady there could deny it, and his life was spared. Then the old woman claimed her reward: he must marry her.

On their wedding night he lay miserable beside her. She offered him a choice: she could be ugly and old and faithful, or young and beautiful and take her chances with other men. He thought, sighed, and said that she should choose whatever was best for them both. Since he had given her the mastery, she said, she would be both beautiful and faithful. He looked and saw a lovely young woman.
lesson: A marriage changes when one partner stops trying to control and gives the other real choice. Respect for the other's judgment can transform the relationship.
people: A knight, an old woman, the queen, King Arthur
source: Geoffrey Chaucer, The Canterbury Tales, The Wife of Bath's Tale
caveat: The tale opens with a rape that the story treats as the knight's crime; it is a medieval text with medieval assumptions.
